# Four-Function Calculator
Clean, high-precision basic calculator for everyday arithmetic.
# How the Four-Function Calculator Works
Behind its four operations — add, subtract, multiply, divide — this calculator follows the same rules you learned in school: multiplication and division are worked out before addition and subtraction, and equal-priority steps run left to right. It also uses high-precision decimal arithmetic, so money math like 19.99 + 4.99 comes out exact instead of a long trail of 9s.
# Worked Example: 48 ÷ 6 × 3 + 12
Divide first: 48 ÷ 6 = 8, so the expression becomes 8 × 3 + 12.
Multiply next: 8 × 3 = 24, leaving 24 + 12.
Add last: 24 + 12 = 36.
Type the whole expression exactly as written and press = — the calculator applies the order of operations for you, so there is no need to break the problem into pieces on paper first.

chunks.title: Percentage Calculator - Free Online Percent Calculator
chunks.text:
# Percentage Calculator
Find X% of Y, what percent X is of Y, and percentage change — instantly and free.
Step 1 : Convert the percent to a decimal: 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2
Step 2 : Multiply by the value: 0.2 × 150 = 30
# How to Calculate Percentages
A percentage is simply a fraction out of 100 — the word itself comes from the Latin per centum , meaning “by the hundred.” Percentages show up everywhere: store discounts, tips, exam grades, interest rates, and statistics. There are three calculations most people need, and this tool handles all of them.
# The Three Percentage Formulas
X% of Y: (X ÷ 100) × Y. Example: 20% of 150 = 0.20 × 150 = 30.
X as a percent of Y: (X ÷ Y) × 100. Example: 30 is (30 ÷ 150) × 100 = 20% of 150.
Percentage change: ((New − Old) ÷ Old) × 100. A price rising from $100 to $125 is a 25% increase.
Shopping sales (“30% off”), restaurant tips, grade calculations, and salary raises all come down to these same three formulas. Once you see the pattern, you can estimate most percentages mentally: 10% of anything is just moving the decimal point one place left.
# Percent vs. Percentage Points

chunks.title: Percentage Calculator - Free Online Percent Calculator
chunks.text:
One common trap: if an interest rate rises from 5% to 7%, that is a 2 percentage point increase — but a 40% percent increase relative to the original 5%. News headlines mix these up constantly. When comparing two percentages, always check which one the writer means.
Need quick arithmetic for the steps above? Try our four-function calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# How do I calculate 20% of 150?
Multiply 150 by 0.20 (which is 20 ÷ 100) to get 30. In general, X% of Y equals (X ÷ 100) × Y — the calculator above does this instantly.
# How do I find what percentage one number is of another?
Divide the first number by the second and multiply by 100. For example, 30 as a percentage of 150 is (30 ÷ 150) × 100 = 20%.
# How do I calculate percentage increase or decrease?
Subtract the old value from the new value, divide by the old value, then multiply by 100. A positive result is an increase; a negative result is a decrease.

chunks.title: Average Calculator - Mean, Median, Mode Online Free
chunks.text:
Mean, median, mode, range — every summary stat for your data set.
Mean: sum ÷ count = 108 ÷ 6 = 18
Median: middle of sorted list [ 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42 ] = 15.5
Range: max − min = 42 − 4 = 38
# Mean, Median, Mode: Which Average?
“Average” usually means the mean — add everything up and divide by how many numbers there are. But the mean is only one way to summarize data, and it can mislead when a few extreme values pull it away from the typical case.
Mean: sum ÷ count. Best for symmetric data without outliers (test scores, measurements).
Median: the middle value when sorted. Best for skewed data like incomes or house prices.
Mode: the most common value. Best for categories — the most popular shoe size, the most common exam answer.
The range (max − min) is the quickest measure of spread: two classes can share a mean of 75 while one ranges 70–80 and the other 40–100. Always pair an average with a sense of spread before drawing conclusions.

# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is the difference between mean, median, and mode?

chunks.title: Average Calculator - Mean, Median, Mode Online Free

The mean is the sum divided by the count; the median is the middle value of the sorted list; the mode is the most frequent value. For 2, 3, 3, 9: the mean is 4.25, the median is 3, and the mode is 3.
# When should I use the median instead of the mean?
Use the median when outliers skew the data — for example, house prices or incomes, where one mansion or billionaire would drag the mean far from the typical value. The median resists outliers.
# Can a data set have more than one mode?
Yes. If two or more values tie for the highest frequency, the data set is bimodal or multimodal — this calculator lists every mode. If all values appear once, there is no mode.

chunks.title: Rounding Calculator - Round to Decimals & Sig Figs Free
chunks.text:
Decimals, significant figures, nearest 10/100/1000, floor & ceiling.
Look at digit 3 after the decimal: 3.14159 → 3.14
Rounding replaces a number with a simpler nearby value. You round when exact precision doesn’t matter — estimating a bill, reporting a measurement, or cleaning up a long decimal — and the key skill is choosing how much precision to keep.
# Decimal Places vs. Significant Figures
Decimal places count digits after the point: 3.14159 to 2 decimals is 3.14. Significant figures count meaningful digits from the first non-zero digit: 0.004567 to 3 sig figs is 0.00457. Scientists prefer sig figs because they reflect real measurement precision.
# Common Rounding Modes
Half up: 2.5 → 3 (the school standard, used by this calculator).
Floor / ceiling: always down or always up — used in pricing, pagination, and capacity planning.
Nearest 10/100/1000: for big-picture estimates — 4,782 to the nearest hundred is 4,800.
Crunching the numbers before rounding? Try our four-function calculator or the scientific calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What are the basic rules of rounding?

chunks.title: Rounding Calculator - Round to Decimals & Sig Figs Free
chunks.text:
Look at the first digit you are dropping: if it is 5 or more, round the last kept digit up; if it is 4 or less, leave it. So 3.146 to two decimals is 3.15, while 3.141 to two decimals is 3.14.
# What are significant figures?
Significant figures count the meaningful digits of a number, starting from the first non-zero digit. 0.00450 has three significant figures (4, 5, 0). They tell you how precise a measurement really is.
# What is the difference between floor and ceiling?
Floor always rounds down to the nearest integer (floor of 4.9 is 4, floor of −4.1 is −5), while ceiling always rounds up (ceiling of 4.1 is 5, ceiling of −4.9 is −4).

# Standard Deviation Calculator
Population & sample SD, variance, and mean — with every step shown.
Step 1: Mean = 40 ÷ 8 = 5
Step 2: Squared deviations from the mean sum to 32
Step 3: Population variance = 32 ÷ 8 = 4
Step 4: Population SD = √ 4 = 2
Step 5: Sample SD divides by n-1 = 7 : √( 32 ÷ 7 ) = 2.1381
# What Standard Deviation Tells You
Standard deviation measures spread : how far numbers typically stray from the average. Two classes can both average 75%, but if one has an SD of 3 and the other 15, the first class is tightly bunched while the second ranges from failing to perfect scores.
# Population vs. Sample: Which One?
Population (σ): you have every value — divide by N.
Sample (s): you have a subset and want to estimate the whole — divide by n−1.
When in doubt for homework, most statistics classes expect the sample version.
For bell-shaped data, about 68% of values fall within one SD of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three. That is why SD is the backbone of grading curves, quality control, and polling margins.
Need the average first? Try our average calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions

chunks.title: Standard Deviation Calculator - Free SD Calculator Online
chunks.text:
# What is the difference between population and sample standard deviation?
Population SD (σ) divides the sum of squared deviations by N and describes a complete dataset. Sample SD (s) divides by n−1 to correct for bias when estimating from a sample.
# How is standard deviation calculated step by step?
Find the mean, subtract it from each value, square each difference, average those squares (this is the variance), then take the square root.
# Why do we divide by n−1 for sample standard deviation?
Dividing by n−1 (Bessel's correction) compensates for the fact that a sample tends to underestimate the true spread of the full population.

# Probability Calculator
Simple, complement, AND & OR probabilities — decimal, percent, and fraction.
Enter probabilities as decimals between 0 and 1 (0.5 = 50%). AND/OR assume independent events.
Step 1 : P(A) = favorable ÷ total = 1 ÷ 6
Step 2 : = 0.166667 = 16.666667% = 1/6
# Probability in Plain English
Probability is just favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes — a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain). A coin flip is 0.5, a specific lottery ticket is roughly 1 in 300 million. Everything else is built from that one idea.
# The Four Rules on This Page
Simple: P(A) = favorable ÷ total.
Complement: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) — sometimes the “not” is easier to compute.
AND (independent): multiply — P(A)×P(B). Two coin flips both heads: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25.
OR (independent): add, then subtract the overlap — P(A)+P(B)−P(A)×P(B).
People add probabilities for AND (“10% and 10% = 20%”) — wrong. Two independent 10% events both happening is 0.1 × 0.1 = 1% , not 20%. Multiplication shrinks; addition grows. When in doubt, the calculator keeps you honest.
Counting the outcomes first? Our factorial calculator handles permutations and combinations.
# Frequently Asked Questions

chunks.title: Probability Calculator - P(A), AND/OR & Complement
chunks.text:
# What is the basic probability formula?
P(A) = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. Rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.1667, or about 16.67%.
# How do you calculate AND vs OR probability?
For independent events, multiply for AND: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). For OR, use P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A)×P(B) so shared outcomes are not double-counted.
# What is complement probability?
The complement is everything except the event: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). If rain has a 25% chance, no rain has a 75% chance.

5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120
Definition: n! = n × (n−1) × … × 2 × 1, with 0! = 1 by definition.
Uses: counting permutations and combinations in probability and statistics.
# Where Factorials Come From
Ask “in how many orders can 5 books sit on a shelf?” — the first slot has 5 choices, the next 4, then 3, 2, 1. That is 5! = 120 . Factorials count permutations , and they explode fast: 10! is already 3.6 million, and 20! exceeds 2 quintillion.
# The Two Facts That Confuse Everyone
0! = 1 by definition — an empty product equals 1, which keeps combination formulas working.
Factorials only apply to whole numbers. For decimals, mathematicians extend the idea with the Gamma function, where n! = Γ(n+1).
# Factorials in Probability
Combinations (nCr) and permutations (nPr) are built from factorials — lottery odds, poker hands, and committee selections all reduce to factorial division. Try the probability calculator to put them to work.
# Frequently Asked Questions
The factorial of n (written n!) is the product of all positive integers from 1 to n. For example, 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.
# What is 0 factorial (0!)?

# What Makes a Number Prime
Primes are the atoms of arithmetic : every whole number greater than 1 is either prime or a unique product of primes (the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic). They secure your bank transactions, generate secure keys, and still hide unsolved mysteries — nobody knows if there are infinitely many twin primes.
# The Trial Division Shortcut
To test n, you only need to trial-divide up to √n . Why? If n had a factor larger than √n, its partner factor would be smaller than √n — and you would already have found that one. For 97, that means testing just 2, 3, 5, and 7.
# Special Cases to Memorize
1 is neither prime nor composite.
2 is the only even prime — every other even number is divisible by 2.
0 and negatives are not prime by definition.

# How to Solve Algebra Problems Step by Step
Algebra forms the foundation of advanced mathematics, engineering, and data science. Solving an algebraic equation requires balancing both sides of the equals sign while isolating unknown variables.
Addition / Subtraction Property: You can add or subtract the same value from both sides of the equation without changing the equality ($x - 5 = 10 \implies x = 15$).
Multiplication / Division Property: Multiplying or dividing both sides by a non-zero number maintains balance ($3x = 12 \implies x = 4$).
Distributive Property: Expand terms inside brackets prior to isolating the variable ($a(b + c) = ab + ac$).

chunks.title: Equation Solver - Linear Equations with Step-by-Step
chunks.text:
Find roots and solutions for single-variable linear and algebraic equations with clear steps.
# Solving Linear Equations
A linear equation is an algebraic equation in which each term has an exponent of 1. When graphed, linear equations produce straight lines on the Cartesian plane.
# Standard Solving Procedure:
Eliminate parentheses using the distributive law.
Combine like terms on both sides of the equal sign.
Use addition or subtraction to collect variable terms on one side and constant terms on the other.
Divide or multiply to solve for the coefficient of $x$.
Substitute the result back into original equation to verify correctness.
# Worked Example: 3(x − 2) = 2x + 5
Distribute: 3x − 6 = 2x + 5.
Collect the x terms: subtract 2x from both sides → x − 6 = 5.
Isolate x: add 6 to both sides → x = 11.
Check: 3(11 − 2) = 27 and 2(11) + 5 = 27. Both sides match, so x = 11 is correct.
# When There Is No Single Answer

chunks.title: Equation Solver - Linear Equations with Step-by-Step
chunks.text:
Not every equation ends with one number. If the x terms cancel and leave a false statement like 4 = 9, the equation has no solution — no value of x can make it true. If they cancel and leave a true statement like 7 = 7, the equation is an identity and every real number is a solution. The solver above reports these cases instead of forcing a number, which is exactly the answer your teacher is looking for when a problem is designed to have none.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# How do I solve 5x - 15 = 35 step by step?
Add 15 to both sides to get 5x = 50, then divide both sides by 5 to get x = 10. The solver above shows each step automatically.
# Can it solve equations with x on both sides?
Yes — enter equations like 5x - 3 = 2x + 9 and the solver collects the x-terms on one side before isolating the variable.

chunks.title: Quadratic Equation Solver - Solve ax²+bx+c=0 Step by Step
chunks.text:
# Quadratic Equation Solver
Roots, discriminant, and vertex of ax² + bx + c = 0 — with every step shown.
Step 1 : Discriminant: D = b² − 4ac = (-3)² − 4(1)(2) = 1
Step 2 : Since D > 0, there are two distinct real roots.
Step 3 : x = [−(-3) ± √(1)] ÷ (2 × 1)
Step 4 : x₁ = 4 ÷ 2 = 2
Step 5 : x₂ = 2 ÷ 2 = 1
# How to Solve Quadratic Equations
A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0. Unlike linear equations, quadratics can have zero, one, or two real solutions — and the discriminant , D = b² − 4ac, tells you which case you have before you compute anything.
# Reading the Discriminant
D > 0: two distinct real roots — the parabola crosses the x-axis twice.
D = 0: one repeated root — the vertex just touches the x-axis.
D < 0: no real roots — the solutions are a pair of complex conjugates.
# The Quadratic Formula
Plug a, b, and c into x = (−b ± √D) ÷ 2a. The ± is what produces the two roots. Many students lose marks on sign errors with −b, so write each substitution out — exactly what the step-by-step panel above does for you.

chunks.title: Quadratic Equation Solver - Solve ax²+bx+c=0 Step by Step
chunks.text:
The vertex (−b ÷ 2a) is the parabola's turning point: a minimum when a > 0, a maximum when a < 0. Knowing the vertex plus the roots lets you sketch the entire graph in seconds.
Working with linear equations instead? Try our linear equation solver .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is the quadratic formula?
The quadratic formula is x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a. It gives the solutions of any quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0, and this solver applies it step by step.
# What does a negative discriminant mean?
A negative discriminant (b² − 4ac < 0) means the equation has no real roots — instead it has two complex conjugate roots, which this solver displays.
# How do I find the vertex of a parabola?
The vertex of y = ax² + bx + c is at x = −b ÷ 2a. Substitute that x back into the equation to get the y-coordinate. The solver shows it automatically.

Solve 2×2 and 3×3 linear systems — every elimination step shown.
Step 1 : D = a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = (2)(-1) − (1)(3) = -5
Step 2 : Dx = c₁b₂ − c₂b₁ = -11, Dy = a₁c₂ − a₂c₁ = -6
Step 3 : x = Dx/D = 2.2, y = Dy/D = 1.2
# How to Solve Systems of Equations
A system of equations is a set of equations that share the same variables — the solution is the point (x, y, …) satisfying all of them at once. Two straight lines usually cross at exactly one point; that point is the solution.
Elimination: add or subtract multiples of equations to cancel one variable at a time — the most mechanical method, used for the 3×3 solver above.
Substitution: solve one equation for a variable and plug it into the others — great for 2×2 by hand.
Cramer’s rule: express each variable as a ratio of determinants — elegant for 2×2, shown step by step above.
If elimination produces 0 = 5, the system is inconsistent (no solution — parallel lines). If it produces 0 = 0, the equations are dependent (infinitely many solutions — the same line twice). The calculator detects and reports both.

A linear inequality looks like an equation, except the equals sign is replaced by >, <, ≥, or ≤. Instead of one answer, you get a whole range of answers — every number that makes the statement true. Solving works almost exactly like solving equations, with one famous exception.
# The Golden Rule: Flip on Negatives
Add, subtract, multiply, or divide both sides just like an equation — except when you multiply or divide by a negative number, you must flip the inequality sign. So −3x < 9 becomes x > −3. Forgetting this flip is the #1 mistake students make.
Inequality form: x > 4 — direct and familiar.

Flip the inequality sign whenever you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number. For example, −2x > 6 becomes x < −3 after dividing by −2.

# How Differentiation Works
A derivative measures a function's instantaneous rate of change — the slope of its curve at any point. Differentiation follows a small set of rules, and nearly every problem is solved by recognizing which rules apply and applying them in the right order.
Power Rule: d/dx[xⁿ] = n·xⁿ⁻¹. The workhorse — try it on x³ to get 3x².
Sum Rule: differentiate term by term; constants vanish.
Product Rule: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′ for multiplied functions.
Quotient Rule: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′) / v² for divisions.
Chain Rule: for nested functions like sin(x²) — outer derivative times inner derivative.
Differentiate f(x) = x²·eˣ. The product rule gives (2x)(eˣ) + (x²)(eˣ) = eˣ(2x + x²). Notice the strategy: identify the structure first (a product), then differentiate each piece with the power and exponential rules. The calculator above follows the same logic and names the rules it uses.
Need to evaluate the derivative at a point? Plug values into our scientific calculator .

# What is the chain rule, with an example?
The chain rule differentiates a function inside another function: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f′(g(x)) × g′(x). For sin(x²), the outer derivative cos(x²) is multiplied by the inner derivative 2x, giving 2x·cos(x²).

Factoring means rewriting something as a product of simpler pieces. For integers, the “simplest pieces” are prime numbers; for quadratics, they are linear factors like (x + 2). This free factor calculator does both: enter any integer for its prime factorization, or any quadratic expression to see it factored step by step. # What is prime factorization?

chunks.title: Factor Calculator - Prime Factorization & Factoring Quadratics
chunks.text:

# How Matrix Operations Work
A matrix is a grid of numbers, and a 2×2 matrix packs four values into two rows and two columns. Matrices earn their keep because one grid can describe a whole transformation at once — stretching, rotating, or solving a pair of equations — and the operations above are the ones everything else is built from.
# Worked Example: Multiplying A × B
Take A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]]. Each entry of the product comes from a row of A meeting a column of B:
Top-left: 1×5 + 2×7 = 19
Top-right: 1×6 + 2×8 = 22
Bottom-left: 3×5 + 4×7 = 43
Bottom-right: 3×6 + 4×8 = 50
So A × B = [[19, 22], [43, 50]]. Note that order matters: B × A gives [[23, 34], [31, 46]], a different answer — matrix multiplication is not commutative.
# Determinant and Inverse
The determinant of [[a, b], [c, d]] is ad − bc. For A above, det = 1×4 − 2×3 = −2. The inverse swaps a and d, flips the signs of b and c, and divides everything by the determinant: A⁻¹ = [[−2, 1], [1.5, −0.5]]. If the determinant is 0, no inverse exists — the matrix squashes the plane flat.

A matrix has no inverse when its determinant is zero — it is called singular. The calculator will show an error for singular matrices instead of a wrong answer.
# How do you find the determinant of a 2×2 matrix?
Multiply the diagonal entries and subtract: for [[a, b], [c, d]], det = ad − bc. For [[1, 2], [3, 4]] that is 1×4 − 2×3 = −2. Press det(A) above and the calculator shows the value instantly.
# Can I solve a system of equations with a matrix inverse?
Yes. Write the system as A·x = b, compute A⁻¹ with the Inverse button, then x = A⁻¹b. For x + 2y = 5 and 3x + 4y = 11, A⁻¹ times [5, 11] gives x = 1, y = 2 — the pair that satisfies both equations.

# Fraction Calculator with Steps
Calculate addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of fractions with simplified step-by-step reduction.
# Working with Fractions Explained
Fractions represent parts of a whole, made up of a numerator (top number) and a denominator (bottom number).
# Basic Fraction Operations:
Adding & Subtracting: Requires finding the Least Common Denominator (LCD) before combining the numerators.
Multiplying: Multiply straight across (numerator by numerator, denominator by denominator) without finding common denominators.
Dividing: Multiply by the reciprocal (flip the second fraction and multiply).
# Simplifying to Lowest Terms
Our calculator automatically computes common divisors to simplify fractions into their simplest form.
# Worked Example: 3/4 + 2/5, Step by Step
Find a common denominator: the LCD of 4 and 5 is 20.
Convert both fractions: 3/4 = 15/20 and 2/5 = 8/20.
Add the numerators: 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20.
Convert to a mixed number: 23/20 = 1 3/20 — already in lowest terms, since 23 is prime.
The calculator above performs exactly these steps and shows its working, so you can check your own method against it line by line.

# When Fractions Beat Decimals

Fractions also keep precision that decimals lose: 1/3 is exact, but 0.333 is an approximation that drifts when you multiply it back. Use this tool whenever a problem starts in fractions — homework, scaling a recipe up or down, or adding tape-measure lengths like 5 1/2 + 3 3/4 inches.

# How do you divide fractions?

# LCM and HCF Calculator
Least common multiple and highest common factor — with every step shown.
Step 1 : Find GCD of 18 and 12 using the Euclidean algorithm:
Step 2 : 18 = 12 × 1 + 6
Step 3 : 12 = 6 × 2 + 0
Step 4 : Last non-zero remainder = 6, so GCD(12, 18) = 6.
LCM: ( 12 × 18 × 24 ) ÷ 6 = 72
# How to Find LCM and HCF
The highest common factor (HCF) , also called the greatest common divisor (GCD), is the biggest number that divides every number in your set. The least common multiple (LCM) is the smallest number that is a multiple of every number in the set. They are linked by a neat identity: LCM(a, b) × HCF(a, b) = a × b.
Prime factorization: break each number into primes; the HCF takes the lowest power of each shared prime, the LCM takes the highest power of every prime present.
Euclidean algorithm: repeatedly replace the larger number with the remainder of dividing it by the smaller — the fastest route to the HCF, shown step by step above.
Adding fractions needs the LCM of the denominators; simplifying fractions needs the HCF of numerator and denominator. They also appear in scheduling problems (“two buses leave together — when next?”) and gear-ratio puzzles.

chunks.title: LCM and HCF Calculator - Free GCD Calculator with Steps
chunks.text:

# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is the difference between LCM and HCF?
The HCF (highest common factor, also called GCD) is the largest number that divides all the given numbers exactly. The LCM (least common multiple) is the smallest number that all the given numbers divide into exactly. For 12 and 18, the HCF is 6 and the LCM is 36.
# How do you find the LCM and HCF of three numbers?
Work pairwise: find the GCD of the first two numbers, then the GCD of that result with the third number. For the LCM, use LCM(a, b, c) = LCM(LCM(a, b), c). This calculator handles any count of numbers automatically.
# What is the Euclidean algorithm?
It is the fastest way to find a GCD: divide the larger number by the smaller, replace the larger with the remainder, and repeat until the remainder is zero. The last non-zero remainder is the GCD. The calculator shows each division step.

# How to Simplify Algebraic Expressions
Simplifying an algebraic expression means rewriting it in its most compact equivalent form. The two core moves are combining like terms (terms with the same variable raised to the same power) and expanding brackets with the distributive law.
# The Order of Operations for Simplifying
Clear brackets first: multiply out using the distributive law, e.g. 2(x + 3) becomes 2x + 6.
Combine like terms: 4x + 7x = 11x, but x² and x stay separate — different exponents are not like terms.
Collect constants: plain numbers merge into one, e.g. 8 − 3 = 5.
Most simplification mistakes come from sign errors when expanding brackets: −(x − 4) is −x + 4, not −x − 4. Work slowly through one bracket at a time.
Need to break an expression into factors instead? Try our factoring calculator or the algebra solver .

# What does it mean to simplify an expression?
Simplifying means rewriting an expression in its shortest equivalent form — combining like terms, removing brackets, and cancelling where possible, without changing its value.
# How do you combine like terms?

# Solving Exponential Equations
When the unknown is in the exponent — like 3^x = 81 — logarithms undo the exponent. Take the log of both sides and the exponent drops down: x = log(81) ÷ log(3) = 4. This is exactly how the solve mode works.
# Negative and Fractional Exponents
A negative exponent means “reciprocal”: 2^(−3) = 1/8. A fractional exponent means “root”: 16^(1/2) = √16 = 4. Both follow from the same laws, just run in reverse.
Working with roots and powers together? Try our scientific calculator or learn about the inverse operation with the logarithm calculator .

An exponent tells you how many times to multiply the base by itself. In 2^5, the base is 2 and the exponent is 5, so 2^5 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.

# How to Complete the Square
Completing the square is the algebraic trick behind the quadratic formula itself. The idea: force part of the expression into a perfect square (x + d)², then tidy up whatever is left over.
Normalize: if a ≠ 1, factor a out of the x-terms first.
Halve and square: take half of the x-coefficient, square it — that is the number that completes the square.
Balance: add it inside the brackets and subtract the equivalent outside, then collapse to (x + d)² + k.
In y = a(x − h)² + k, the vertex is (h, k). Watch the sign: (x + 3)² means h = −3. If a > 0 the parabola opens upward and the vertex is a minimum; if a < 0 it opens downward.
Prefer finding roots directly? Try our quadratic equation solver or solve linear equations with the algebra calculator .

# How do you complete the square for x²+bx?

# How to Find the Slope of a Line
Slope measures a line’s steepness: how many units y changes for each unit x changes. A slope of 2 means “up 2, right 1”; a slope of −1/2 means “down 1, right 2”.
Subtract the y-values (rise), subtract the x-values (run), then divide. Keep the point order consistent — (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) gives the same answer whichever point you call “first”.
In y = mx + b the slope is staring at you: it is m. Parallel lines share the same slope; perpendicular lines have slopes that multiply to −1 (negative reciprocals).
Once you have the slope, solve for intercepts with our equation solver or simplify line expressions with the algebra calculator .

# What is the slope formula?
m = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁): the change in y (rise) divided by the change in x (run) between two points.
# What does a zero or undefined slope mean?
Zero slope is a horizontal line (y = constant). Undefined slope is a vertical line (x = constant) — the run is zero, so division is impossible.
# How do you find slope from an equation?

chunks.text:
# Distance Formula Calculator
Distance between points in 2D or 3D — instantly and free.
# How the Distance Formula Works
The distance formula is the Pythagorean theorem in disguise. The horizontal gap between two points is one leg of a right triangle, the vertical gap is the other leg, and the straight-line distance is the hypotenuse.
In 2D you square two differences; in 3D you square three. The pattern extends to any number of dimensions — just keep adding squared coordinate differences under the square root.
# Exact vs. Decimal Answers
Many distances are irrational (like √50). Geometry classes often want the exact radical form, while applied problems want the decimal — this tool shows both.
# Worked Example: From (2, 3) to (6, 6)
Find the horizontal gap: Δx = 6 − 2 = 4.
Find the vertical gap: Δy = 6 − 3 = 3.
Apply Pythagoras: d = √(4² + 3²) = √(16 + 9) = √25 = 5.
That 3-4-5 pattern is worth remembering — it shows up constantly in homework and on job sites. In 3D, add one more squared gap: from (1, 2, 3) to (4, 6, 3), d = √(3² + 4² + 0²) = 5 again.
# Where You Actually Use This

chunks.title: Distance Formula Calculator - 2D and 3D
chunks.text:
Any time a map gives you coordinates instead of roads: the straight-line (“as the crow flies”) distance between two GPS points, the diagonal brace needed to square a deck frame, the range between a game character and a target on a grid, or the displacement in a physics problem. If the two points are cities on a real map, remember this is the flat-plane version — for long distances over the curved Earth, navigation tools switch to great-circle formulas.
The same right-triangle idea powers our Pythagorean theorem calculator — and you can check the arithmetic with the four-function calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is the distance formula?
d = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²] — it is the Pythagorean theorem applied to the horizontal and vertical gaps between two points.
# How do you find distance in 3D?
Add the squared z-difference: d = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)² + (z₂−z₁)²].
# What is the difference between distance and displacement?
Distance is the total path length (always positive); displacement is the straight-line change from start to finish, which is what this formula computes.

chunks.title: Polynomial Calculator - Add, Multiply, Roots
chunks.text:
# Polynomial Calculator
Add, multiply, and find roots of polynomials — instantly and free.
# How to Work with Polynomials
Polynomials are the workhorses of algebra: sums of power terms like 4x³ − x + 9. The degree — the highest exponent — tells you the shape of the graph and the maximum number of roots.
# Arithmetic with Polynomials
Adding and subtracting is just combining like terms across both polynomials. Multiplying means distributing every term — FOIL is simply the 2-term special case of this general rule.
The rational root theorem narrows the search: every rational root looks like p/q where p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient. Test the candidates — any hit is a genuine root.
# Worked Example: Synthetic Division by (x − 1)
Divide P(x) = x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 by (x − 1). Write the coefficients 1, −6, 11, −6 and bring the test value 1:
Bring down the 1 → multiply by 1, add to −6 → −5.
Repeat: multiply −5 by 1, add to 11 → 6.
Finish: multiply 6 by 1, add to −6 → 0.
The remainder is 0, so x = 1 is a root and the quotient x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) reveals the rest: P(x) = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3), with roots 1, 2, and 3.

chunks.title: Polynomial Calculator - Add, Multiply, Roots
chunks.text:
The leading term controls both ends of the graph. An even degree with a positive leading coefficient (like x⁴) rises on both sides; an odd degree (like x³) falls left and rises right; a negative leading coefficient flips those. Knowing the ends in advance tells you whether the roots you found can possibly be all of them — an odd-degree polynomial must cross the axis at least once.
Found a root and want factors? Try our factoring calculator or simplify expressions with the algebra calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is a polynomial?
An expression of variables and coefficients using only addition, subtraction, multiplication, and non-negative integer exponents — like 3x³ − 2x + 7.
# How do you find rational roots?
List ±(factors of the constant term) ÷ (factors of the leading coefficient) and test each. Any rational root must be on that list — the rational root theorem.
# How do you multiply polynomials?
Multiply every term of the first by every term of the second (distribute fully), then combine like terms.

# Rational Expression Calculator
Simplify algebraic fractions with domain checks — instantly and free.
# How to Simplify Rational Expressions
A rational expression is a fraction of polynomials, and simplifying one works exactly like reducing 6/8 to 3/4: factor everything, then cancel what the top and bottom share.
You cannot cancel terms — only factors. In (x²−1)/(x+1), the top factors to (x+1)(x−1), so the (x+1) factor cancels and you are left with x−1. Cancelling the x’s in (x+5)/x would be wrong because x is a term, not a factor.
# Never Forget the Domain
Cancelling (x+1) does not erase the fact that x = −1 made the original denominator zero. Always state excluded values from the original denominator — this tool lists them automatically.
# Worked Example: Simplifying (x² − 9)/(x² − x − 6)
Factor the numerator: x² − 9 is a difference of squares → (x + 3)(x − 3).
Factor the denominator: x² − x − 6 needs two numbers with product −6 and sum −1 → (x − 3)(x + 2).
Cancel the shared factor: (x − 3) appears top and bottom, leaving (x + 3)/(x + 2).
State the domain: the original denominator is zero at x = 3 and x = −2, so the simplified form is (x + 3)/(x + 2) with x ≠ 3, −2.

chunks.title: Rational Expression Calculator - Simplify
chunks.text:
# Multiplying and Dividing Rational Expressions
Multiplication follows the same factor-first rule: factor every numerator and denominator, then cancel diagonally. Division means multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor — flip the second expression, then factor and cancel. In both cases the excluded values grow: collect zeros from every original denominator, not just the final one.
Need the factoring step explained? See our factoring calculator or practice with plain numeric fractions on the fraction calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is a rational expression?
A fraction whose numerator and denominator are polynomials, like (x²−1)/(x+1). It behaves like a numeric fraction, but the “numbers” are expressions.
# How do you simplify one?
Factor the top and bottom completely, cancel factors common to both, and record which x-values the original denominator excluded.
# What are domain restrictions?
Values that make the original denominator zero are excluded from the domain — even if they cancel out during simplification, the original expression was undefined there.

chunks.title: Inverse Function Calculator - Find f Inverse

# Inverse Function Calculator
Find f⁻¹(x) with swap-and-solve steps — instantly and free.
# How to Find an Inverse Function
Inverse functions reverse each other’s work. If doubling then adding one is f(x) = 2x + 1, the inverse subtracts one then halves: f⁻¹(x) = (x−1)/2. Graphically, an inverse is the mirror image across the line y = x.
# The Swap-and-Solve Method
Swap every x with y (and y with x).
Solve the new equation for y — that y is f⁻¹(x).
Verify by composing: f(f⁻¹(x)) must equal x.
# Worked Example: Inverting f(x) = 3x − 6
Solve for y: add 6 → x + 6 = 3y, divide by 3 → y = (x + 6)/3.
Verify: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 3((x + 6)/3) − 6 = x + 6 − 6 = x ✓. The composition collapses to x exactly, so the inverse is confirmed.
Only one-to-one functions have inverses: no two inputs may share an output. The quick check is the horizontal line test — if any horizontal line crosses the graph twice, the function fails. That is why x² has no single inverse over all reals (split it into x ≥ 0 to fix that), while odd roots like ∛x are fine everywhere.
Powers pair with roots, exponentials pair with logarithms (e^x ↔ ln x), and 1/x is its own inverse. Recognizing the pairs saves algebra.

chunks.title: Inverse Function Calculator - Find f Inverse
chunks.text:

# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is an inverse function?
The function that undoes another: if f maps a→b, then f⁻¹ maps b→a. Applying both returns you to the start: f(f⁻¹(x)) = x.
# How do you find an inverse algebraically?
Write y = f(x), swap x and y, then solve for y. That is the entire method — the tool shows it step by step.
# Which functions have inverses?
Only one-to-one functions (each output comes from exactly one input). x² needs its domain restricted to x ≥ 0 before it qualifies.

Yes, free — no sign-up and nothing to install. Enter a function and its inverse is derived and verified by composition, all in your browser.

chunks.title: Function Composition Calculator - (fog)(x) Steps
chunks.text:
# Function Composition Calculator
(f∘g)(x) and (g∘f)(x), expanded — instantly and free.
# How Function Composition Works
Composition chains functions like a production line: g processes x first, then f processes g’s output. The notation (f∘g)(x) is read “f of g of x”, and the rightmost function always acts first.
# Substitution, Not Multiplication
The classic mistake is multiplying the functions instead of substituting. For f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², (f∘g)(x) replaces every x in f with x², giving 2x² + 1 — not 2x³ + x².
(g∘f)(x) for the same pair is (2x+1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1 — completely different. Always substitute in the order the notation demands, innermost first.
# Worked Example: Evaluating (f∘g)(3)
Keep f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x². To find (f∘g)(3), work from the inside out:
Evaluate the inner function: g(3) = 3² = 9.
Feed that result into f: f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19.
Answer: (f∘g)(3) = 19 — which matches substituting first: (f∘g)(x) = 2x² + 1, and 2(3²) + 1 = 19.

chunks.title: Function Composition Calculator - (fog)(x) Steps
chunks.text:
A composition is only defined where both steps work: x must be in g’s domain, and g(x) must be in f’s domain. If g(x) = √x and f(x) = 1/x, then (f∘g)(x) = 1/√x fails at x = 0 even though each function is fine elsewhere — g(0) = 0 lands outside f’s domain. When the calculator returns an expression, check those two checkpoints before trusting it.
Composition is how inverses are verified: try our inverse function calculator or simplify the substituted expressions with the algebra calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is function composition?
Plugging one function’s output into another: (f∘g)(x) means compute g(x) first, then feed the result into f.
# Is (f∘g)(x) the same as (g∘f)(x)?
Almost never — order matters. If f doubles and g squares, (f∘g)(3) = 18 but (g∘f)(3) = 36.
# How do you evaluate a composition?
Substitute the entire inner function wherever x appears in the outer function, then simplify. The tool expands and simplifies automatically.
# Is this calculator free?
Yes — composing functions here is free, with no sign-up and nothing to install. Enter f and g, and the composed function plus step-by-step evaluation happen right on this page.

# Domain and Range Calculator
Enter f(x) to get its domain and range in interval notation, with reasoning.
# How to Find the Domain and Range of a Function
The domain is the set of all x-values a function can accept, and the range is the set of all y-values it can produce. Three things can break a domain: division by zero, an even root of a negative number, and a logarithm of a non-positive number. Check for those three first, and most domain problems solve themselves.
# Interval Notation Basics
Parentheses ( ) exclude an endpoint: (2, 5) means 2 < x < 5.
Brackets [ ] include an endpoint: [0, ∞) means x ≥ 0.
Infinity always gets a parenthesis: (−∞, ∞) is the whole real line.
For a parabola, complete the square to find the vertex — the range starts or ends there. For 1/x style rational functions, the range is everything except the horizontal asymptote value. When in doubt, sketch the graph: the range is simply how far the curve stretches vertically.
Working with equations? Try our linear equation solver or the derivative calculator to locate maxima and minima.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is the domain of a function?

chunks.title: Domain and Range Calculator - Function Domain Finder
chunks.text:
The domain is the set of all x-values for which the function is defined. Exclude values that make a denominator zero, a square root negative, or a logarithm non-positive.
# What is the range of a function?
The range is the set of all possible output (y) values. For a parabola use the vertex; for 1/x the range is all real numbers except 0.
# How do you write domain in interval notation?
Use parentheses for excluded endpoints and brackets for included ones. For example, [0, ∞) means all x greater than or equal to 0.

chunks.text:
Find antiderivatives term by term — each integration rule shown.
# How Indefinite Integrals Work
An indefinite integral finds the antiderivative of a function — the function whose derivative gives back the original. Because differentiating kills constant terms, every antiderivative comes with an unknown constant + C . The power rule does most of the heavy lifting: ∫x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1), for any n except −1.
Power rule: ∫x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C (n ≠ −1).
Special case: ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C.
Exponentials: ∫e^x dx = e^x + C; ∫a^x dx = a^x/ln(a) + C.
Trigonometry: ∫sin(x) dx = −cos(x) + C; ∫cos(x) dx = sin(x) + C.
Constant multiple: ∫k·f(x) dx = k·∫f(x) dx — pull constants out first.
# Beyond the Basic Table
Products, quotients, and compositions need substitution, parts, or partial fractions — techniques this table does not attempt. For a numeric answer over an interval, use our definite integral calculator instead. To check an answer, differentiate it with our derivative calculator — you should get the integrand back.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is an indefinite integral?

chunks.title: Integral Calculator - Indefinite Integrals with Steps
chunks.text:
It is the antiderivative of a function — the family of functions whose derivative equals the integrand. It always includes an unknown constant + C.
# What is the power rule for integration?
∫x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n ≠ −1. For example, ∫x² dx = x³/3 + C.
# Why is there always a + C?
Differentiation turns every constant into zero, so reversing it cannot recover the original constant. The + C represents all possible constants.

chunks.title: Definite Integral Calculator - Numeric Integration
chunks.text:
# Definite Integral Calculator
Numeric integration with Simpson's rule — subinterval working shown.
# How Definite Integrals Are Computed
A definite integral ∫ a b f(x) dx measures the signed area under the curve between x = a and x = b. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says: find an antiderivative F, then compute F(b) − F(a). When no elementary antiderivative exists, Simpson's rule approximates the area by fitting parabolas through sample points — with 1000 subintervals, the result is accurate far beyond what homework requires.
# Simpson's Rule in One Line
Split [a, b] into an even number n of slices of width h. Then ∫f ≈ (h/3)·[f(x₀) + 4f(x₁) + 2f(x₂) + 4f(x₃) + … + f(xₙ)]. The alternating 4-2-4 weights are what make it far more accurate than simple rectangles or trapezoids.
Where the antiderivative is a standard form (powers, sin, cos, e^x), this tool also shows the exact value for comparison. For symbolic antiderivatives in general, try our indefinite integral calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is a definite integral?
It is the signed area under f(x) between two limits a and b, computed as F(b) − F(a) where F is any antiderivative of f.

chunks.title: Definite Integral Calculator - Numeric Integration
chunks.text:
# What is Simpson's rule?
A numerical integration method that approximates the area using parabolas through sample points: ∫f ≈ (h/3)[f(x₀) + 4f(x₁) + 2f(x₂) + … + f(xₙ)] with an even number of subintervals.
# How accurate is the numeric result?
With 1000 subintervals, Simpson's rule is accurate to many decimal places for smooth functions. It is still an approximation, not a symbolic proof.

chunks.title: Limit Calculator - Two-Sided Numeric Limits
chunks.text:
Two-sided numeric approach tables — finite points and infinity.
# How Limits Are Evaluated Numerically
A limit asks: what value does f(x) get close to as x gets close to a — without ever needing to equal a? This tool builds an approach table : it evaluates the function at points like a ± 0.1, a ± 0.01, a ± 0.001, and watches where the outputs settle. If the left and right sides settle on the same number, that is (almost certainly) the limit.
Try (x²−1)/(x−1) as x → 1. Direct substitution gives 0/0, but the table shows values homing in on 2 — the hole in the graph is “filled” by the limit. Factoring the numerator first, (x−1)(x+1)/(x−1) = x+1, confirms it exactly.
Jump: left and right approach different numbers — the two-sided limit does not exist.
Blow-up: values grow without bound near a vertical asymptote — the limit is ±∞ (or does not exist as a finite number).
Oscillation: sin(1/x) near 0 never settles — no limit.
Limits are the foundation of derivatives — see our derivative calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is a limit in calculus?

chunks.title: Limit Calculator - Two-Sided Numeric Limits
chunks.text:
A limit is the value a function approaches as the input approaches some point. It describes behavior near the point, even if the function is undefined exactly there.
# What does 0/0 mean in a limit?
It is an indeterminate form — the limit could be anything. Try factoring, rationalizing, or L'Hôpital's rule; numerically, an approach table usually reveals the answer.
# When does a limit not exist?
When the left and right sides approach different values, when the function oscillates forever, or when it grows without bound near a vertical asymptote.

chunks.text:
# Partial Derivative Calculator
Differentiate f(x, y, …) with respect to one variable — others held constant.
# How Partial Derivatives Work
A partial derivative measures how a multivariable function changes when you vary one variable while freezing the others. The notation ∂f/∂x reads “the partial of f with respect to x” — and every other variable is treated as a plain constant during the differentiation.
# The Constant Rule in Action
For f(x, y) = x²y + sin(y): differentiating with respect to x treats y as a constant, so ∂f/∂x = 2xy. Differentiating with respect to y treats x as a constant, giving ∂f/∂y = x² + cos(y). The same power, product, and chain rules from single-variable calculus all still apply.
Partial derivatives power gradient descent in machine learning, heat and wave equations in physics, and marginal analysis in economics. For single-variable differentiation, see our derivative calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is a partial derivative?
It is the derivative of a multivariable function with respect to one variable, treating all other variables as constants. Written ∂f/∂x for differentiation with respect to x.
# How do you treat other variables?

chunks.title: Partial Derivative Calculator - Differentiate f(x,y)
chunks.text:
As constants. In x²y + sin(y), differentiating with respect to x treats y as a constant, giving 2xy.
# What is the difference between d/dx and ∂/∂x?
d/dx is the ordinary derivative of a single-variable function; ∂/∂x is the partial derivative, used when the function depends on several variables.

chunks.title: Implicit Differentiation Calculator - Find dy/dx
chunks.text:
# Implicit Differentiation Calculator
dy/dx for equations like x² + y² = 25 — via −Fx/Fy, steps shown.
# How Implicit Differentiation Works
Some curves cannot be written as y = (something with only x) — think of a circle x² + y² = 25. Implicit differentiation differentiates both sides of the equation as written, remembering that y is secretly a function of x (so differentiating y² gives 2y·dy/dx by the chain rule), then solves for dy/dx.
Write the equation as F(x, y) = 0. Then dy/dx = −F x /F y , where F x and F y are the ordinary partial derivatives. For the circle: F x = 2x, F y = 2y, so dy/dx = −x/y — exactly the slope of the tangent at any point on the circle.
The formula needs F y ≠ 0. At points where F y = 0 the tangent is vertical and dy/dx is undefined. For ordinary single-variable derivatives, see our derivative calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is implicit differentiation?
It differentiates both sides of an equation like x² + y² = 25 without first solving for y, using the chain rule on y-terms, then solves the result for dy/dx.
# What is the formula for dy/dx?

chunks.title: Implicit Differentiation Calculator - Find dy/dx
chunks.text:
Write the equation as F(x,y) = 0. Then dy/dx = −Fx/Fy, where Fx and Fy are the partial derivatives of F. For the circle this gives dy/dx = −x/y.
# When does implicit differentiation fail?
When Fy = 0 at the point of interest — the tangent is vertical there, so dy/dx is undefined.

chunks.title: Taylor Series Calculator - Polynomial Expansion
chunks.text:
# Taylor Series Calculator
Term-by-term Taylor/Maclaurin polynomials from symbolic derivatives.
# How Taylor Series Work
A Taylor series rewrites a smooth function as an infinite polynomial built from its derivatives at a single point: f(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x−a) + f″(a)(x−a)²/2! + … Each term corrects the approximation using higher-order information about how the function curves. Stop after n terms and you get the Taylor polynomial of degree n.
# Maclaurin: The Special Case a = 0
Center at zero and the series is called a Maclaurin series . The famous ones: e^x = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + …, sin(x) = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …, cos(x) = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − …. These power series are how calculators themselves evaluate transcendental functions internally.
A Taylor polynomial approximates well near the center; far away it can diverge wildly. The interval where the full series converges must be checked separately — try our series convergence calculator for that, or the derivative calculator for the underlying derivatives.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is a Taylor series?

chunks.title: Taylor Series Calculator - Polynomial Expansion
chunks.text:
It represents a smooth function as an infinite sum of polynomial terms built from its derivatives at one point: f(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x−a) + f″(a)(x−a)²/2! + …
# What is a Maclaurin series?
A Taylor series centered at a = 0. Famous examples: e^x = 1 + x + x²/2! + …, sin(x) = x − x³/3! + ….
# How accurate is a Taylor polynomial?
Very accurate near the center, improving with degree. Far from the center it can diverge — always check the interval of convergence.

chunks.title: Series Convergence Calculator - Test Infinite Series
chunks.text:
# Series Convergence Calculator
nth-term, geometric, p-series, ratio, and root tests — conditions checked.
# How Series Convergence Tests Work
An infinite series Σa_n converges if its partial sums settle toward a finite number — otherwise it diverges. No single test handles every series, so mathematicians built a toolbox. The strategy: try the cheapest test first and escalate only when it comes back inconclusive.
nth-term test: if a_n does not → 0, the series diverges. (Passing it proves nothing.)
Geometric: Σar^(n−1) converges iff |r| < 1, summing to a/(1−r).
p-series: Σ1/n^p converges iff p > 1 — the harmonic series (p = 1) famously diverges.
Ratio test: if |a_(n+1)/a_n| → L < 1, converges; L > 1, diverges; L = 1, inconclusive.
Root test: same logic with |a_n|^(1/n) — best for terms with nth powers.
Series are the engine behind Taylor expansions — see our Taylor series calculator .
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What does it mean for a series to converge?
The partial sums approach a finite number. For example, 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … converges to 1, while 1 + 2 + 3 + … diverges.
# What is the ratio test?

chunks.title: Series Convergence Calculator - Test Infinite Series
chunks.text:
Compute L = lim |a_(n+1)/a_n|. If L < 1 the series converges absolutely; if L > 1 it diverges; if L = 1 the test is inconclusive.
# Does the harmonic series converge?
No — Σ 1/n diverges even though its terms approach 0. It is the classic proof that terms → 0 is not enough for convergence.

Step 2 : Angle B similarly = 53.13°, then C = 180° − A − B = 90°
Step 3 : Semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c) / 2 = 6; area = √[s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)] = 6
# How to Solve a Triangle
“Solving” a triangle means finding every unknown side and angle from the ones you know. You always need three pieces of data, and at least one of them must be a side — three angles alone only fix the shape, not the size.
SSS (three sides): angles come from the law of cosines, e.g. cos A = (b² + c² − a²) / 2bc.
SAS (two sides + included angle): the third side comes from the law of cosines, then the law of sines finishes the angles.
ASA (two angles + included side): the third angle is 180° minus the other two, then the law of sines gives the remaining sides.
Not every trio of numbers makes a triangle: sides 2, 3, 10 violate the triangle inequality. And SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) is the famous ambiguous case that can yield zero, one, or two valid triangles — a deeper topic for another day.

Once all three sides are known, the calculator uses Heron's formula: area = √[s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)] where s is the semi-perimeter. For SAS input it can also use ½ab·sin(C).

a= 3 b= 4 c= 5 c = 5 Step 1 : a² + b² = c² → 3² + 4² = c²
Step 2 : c² = 9 + 16 = 25
In any right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the two legs. It is one of the oldest and most useful facts in mathematics — builders use the 3-4-5 triangle to square up foundations, and GPS systems solve millions of triangle problems per second.
# Solving for Each Side
Hypotenuse: c = √(a² + b²) — square, add, square-root.
A leg: a = √(c² − b²) — subtract first, then square-root. The hypotenuse must be the longest side.
Some integer sets fit perfectly: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), and (7, 24, 25). Spotting a multiple of one of these triples lets you answer without a calculator — a favorite trick in timed exams.

# What is the Pythagorean theorem formula?
a² + b² = c², where a and b are the legs of a right triangle and c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle).
# How do you find the hypotenuse with two sides?

Plug the three sides into a² + b² = c² with the longest side as c. If both sides of the equation match, the triangle is right-angled.

# Trigonometry Essentials
Trigonometry studies the relationships between angles and sides in triangles. For a right triangle, three ratios do all the work: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse , cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse , tan θ = opposite/adjacent — remembered with the mnemonic SOH-CAH-TOA.
On a circle of radius 1, the coordinates of any angle are simply (cos θ, sin θ). The exact values at 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90° come from splitting equilateral triangles and squares — memorize those four and you can derive the rest with symmetry. The table above lists every standard angle.

A 10-meter ladder leans against a wall at 65° to the ground. How far is the foot from the wall? The ladder is the hypotenuse, the ground is the adjacent side, and cos(65°) = adjacent / 10:
Pick the ratio: we know the hypotenuse and want the adjacent side → cosine.

# How Compound Interest Works
Compound interest is interest calculated on both the initial principal and the accumulated interest of previous periods — “interest on interest.” It is the engine behind savings accounts, retirement funds, and long-term investing, and also the reason unpaid credit-card debt snowballs so aggressively.
# The Formula, Explained
A = P(1 + r/n) nt : start with principal P, add each period’s interest at rate r/n, and repeat nt times. More frequent compounding means each period’s interest starts earning sooner — try switching between yearly and monthly above to see the gap.
A handy mental shortcut: divide 72 by your annual rate to estimate doubling time. At 6%, money doubles in about 12 years; at 9%, in about 8. Time matters more than most people expect — starting ten years earlier can matter more than a higher rate.

# What is the difference between compound and simple interest?
Simple interest pays only on the original principal, while compound interest pays on the principal plus all previously earned interest — so the balance grows faster every period. Over long time spans the difference is enormous.
# Does compounding frequency really matter?
Yes, but less than the rate and time. Monthly compounding beats yearly compounding at the same nominal rate because interest starts earning its own interest sooner. Daily compounding adds only a little more on top.

# How Loan EMI Is Calculated
EMI — equated monthly installment — is the fixed amount you pay your lender every month until a loan is fully repaid. Each payment covers that month's interest first, and whatever is left reduces the principal. Early in the loan you pay mostly interest; near the end you pay mostly principal.
EMI = P x r x (1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n - 1)
P is the loan amount.
r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate divided by 12).
n is the number of monthly payments.
A $300,000 home loan at 7% annual interest for 30 years (360 months): r = 0.07/12 = 0.00583, giving an EMI of about $1,996. Over 30 years you would pay roughly $418,500 in interest alone — more than the loan itself. Shortening the tenure raises the EMI but slashes total interest.
Compare the total interest , not just the EMI, when choosing between offers. Even a 0.5% lower rate saves tens of thousands on a long loan, and making one extra payment a year can cut years off the schedule. # Understanding Your GPA
GPA (Grade Point Average) condenses your academic performance into a single number on the standard 4.0 scale, where an A equals 4.0 and an F equals 0.0. Because courses carry different credit hours, GPA is a weighted average: a 4-credit course influences your GPA more than a 1-credit lab.

Most courses do not treat every assignment equally. A final exam might count for 30% of your grade while weekly homework counts for 10%. Your course grade is a weighted average : each score is multiplied by its weight, the products are added, and the total is divided by the sum of the weights.

26 >= 10 (X) -> append "X", remainder 16
16 >= 10 (X) -> append "X", remainder 6
6 >= 5 (V) -> append "V", remainder 1

# How Roman Numerals Work
Roman numerals use seven letters — I, V, X, L, C, D, M — for 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, and 1000. Values are normally added left to right, but a smaller value before a larger one means subtraction: IV is 4, IX is 9, XL is 40, CM is 900.
Only I, X, and C can be used subtractively (IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, CM).
V, L, D are never subtracted.
No symbol repeats more than three times in a row (so 4 is IV, not IIII).
# Converting Step by Step
To convert 2026: take the largest symbol that fits — M (1000) twice leaves 26; then X (10) twice leaves 6; then V (5) leaves 1; then I. Result: MMXXVI. The converter above shows this greedy breakdown for every number, and reverses the process just as easily.

# How Number Bases Work
Everyday numbers are base 10 (decimal): each digit is worth ten times the one to its right. Computers use base 2 (binary) because circuits have two states, and programmers use base 16 (hexadecimal) as a compact shorthand — one hex digit represents exactly four binary digits.
# Converting Between Bases
To decimal: multiply each digit by the base raised to its position and add up. Binary 1011 = 1x8 + 0x4 + 1x2 + 1x1 = 11.
From decimal: repeatedly divide by the target base and read the remainders backwards.
Binary to hex shortcut: group binary digits in fours and convert each group (1010 1111 = AF).
# Why Programmers Love Hex
Memory addresses, color codes (#FF5733), and Unicode values are all written in hex because it is far shorter than binary but converts to it trivially. A single byte (0–255) is always exactly two hex digits.

# What is hexadecimal used for?
Memory addresses, HTML color codes, Unicode code points, and MAC addresses are commonly written in hexadecimal because it is compact and converts cleanly to binary.

# How to Solve Linear Equations Step by Step
By the Math Solver Free Editorial Team · Last reviewed: October 2026
A linear equation is an equation where the unknown (usually called x ) appears only to the first power — no x², no square roots. If you can solve these confidently, you've unlocked the foundation of all algebra.
The goal is always the same: isolate x on one side of the equals sign. Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other. That's the entire game.
Simplify each side — clear brackets and combine like terms.
Move the x-terms to one side — add or subtract terms from both sides.
Move the numbers to the other side — same idea, opposite side.
Divide to isolate x — divide both sides by the coefficient of x.
# Worked example 1: 2x + 5 = 13
Step 1: Nothing to simplify — move straight on.
Step 2: The x-term is already alone on the left.
Step 3: Subtract 5 from both sides: 2x + 5 − 5 = 13 − 5 → 2x = 8 .
Step 4: Divide both sides by 2: x = 8 ÷ 2 → x = 4 .
Check: substitute back: 2(4) + 5 = 8 + 5 = 13 ✓
# Worked example 2 (with fractions): x/3 + 2 = 7
Step 3: Subtract 2 from both sides: x/3 = 5.
Step 4: Multiply both sides by 3: x = 15.
Check: 15/3 + 2 = 5 + 2 = 7 ✓

chunks.title: Solve Linear Equations Step by Step (With Examples)
chunks.text:
Fractions scare people, but the steps are identical — clearing the denominator (multiplying both sides by 3) is just step 4 with multiplication instead of division.
# Worked example 3 (x on both sides): 5x − 3 = 2x + 9
Step 2: Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x − 3 = 9.
Step 3: Add 3 to both sides: 3x = 12.
Step 4: Divide by 3: x = 4 .
Check: 5(4) − 3 = 17; 2(4) + 9 = 17 ✓
# Common mistakes to avoid
Forgetting to apply an operation to both sides. If you subtract 5 from the left, you must subtract 5 from the right too.
Sign errors when moving terms. Moving +2x to the other side makes it −2x. Write the sign change explicitly until it's automatic.
Dividing only part of the expression. In (2x + 8) ÷ 2, BOTH terms get divided: x + 4, not x + 8.
Skipping the check. Thirty seconds of substitution catches most errors — always do it in exams.
# Frequently asked questions
# What is a linear equation in simple terms?
An equation where the variable appears only to the first power, like 3x + 2 = 11. Its graph is always a straight line.
# How do I check my answer?
Substitute your x value back into the original equation. If both sides are equal, your answer is correct.
# What if x is on both sides?

chunks.text:

# October 2026 SAT Math Answers Explained (With Steps)
October 20, 2026 · Math Solver Free Team
Short on time? Here are the answers students argued about most. The viral "p/1000" percent-chain question: 600 cartons remain. The population that grew by 150% and then fell by 50%: a 25% overall increase , not 100%. The radical equation √(x + 5) = x − 1: x = 4 only — x = −1 is extraneous. And where y = x² − 4x + 3 meets y = −x + 7, the product of the x-coordinates is −4 . Below is the full working for each question, why the popular wrong answers are wrong, and how to check all of them in Desmos in seconds.
# Why the October 2026 SAT math section sparked so much debate
The October 3, 2026 SAT ended on a Saturday afternoon, but for thousands of students the test was only half over. Within hours, test-takers from both the US and International versions flooded Reddit to compare answers — and on several math questions the comment sections split wide open. On October 4, TheTestAdvantage published a solved set of 24 of the most contested October SAT Math questions crowdsourced from those Reddit threads, finally giving the debate an answer key to argue against.

chunks.title: October 2026 SAT Math Answers Explained (With Steps)
chunks.text:
The most viral thread was the "p/1000" percent-chain question: 53 students weighed in, answers clustering around 600, 550, 650, and 700. Only one is correct. Below: the hardest debated types with full solutions, why each wrong answer tempted capable students, and Desmos tips that settle these debates in seconds. One honest note: the live items cannot be republished, so each worked problem is a representative reconstruction of the debated type. The numbers are illustrative; the math and the traps are real.
# October 2026 SAT math answers: the viral "p/1000" percent-chain question
Here is a representative reconstruction of the debated type:
Representative problem: A warehouse stocks 1,000 cartons of milk. On Monday, 25% of the cartons are sold. On Tuesday, 20% of the remaining cartons are sold. How many cartons remain after Tuesday?
Reddit dubbed it the "p/1000" question: the clean solution writes each percent as p/100 and chains the multiplications from a base of 1,000.
# Step-by-step solution
Convert Monday's percent to a "stays" multiplier. Selling 25% leaves 75%: 75/100 = 0.75, so Monday's remainder is (75/100) × 1,000.
Compute Monday's remainder: 0.75 × 1,000 = 750 cartons.

chunks.title: October 2026 SAT Math Answers Explained (With Steps)
chunks.text:
Convert Tuesday's percent the same way. Selling 20% of the remainder leaves 80%: (80/100) × 750.
Compute Tuesday's remainder: 0.80 × 750 = 600. Answer: 600 — one chain: (75/100) × (80/100) × 1,000 = 600.
# Why 550, 650, and 700 each tempted students
550 — the "add the percents" trap. The most common SAT percent mistake: 25% + 20% = 45%, so 45% of 1,000 = 450 sold, leaving 550. But sequential percents never add — each acts on a new, smaller base. If you catch yourself adding chained percents, stop: that is the trap the question was built around.
700 — the "wrong base" trap. These students found Monday's 750 but applied Tuesday's 20% to the wrong quantity — for example, 20% of Monday's sold cartons (20% of 250 = 50), subtracted from 750, gives 700. The word "remaining" does all the work here: Tuesday's percent applies to the 750 cartons still on the shelves.
650 — the "stale base" trap. These students knew to chain but grabbed a stale number: subtracting 20% of 500 (= 100) from 750 gives 650. After every step, ask "20% of what, exactly?" and recompute the base.
# A second debated trap: chained percent change
The same "never add percents" lesson appeared in a second debated type:

chunks.title: October 2026 SAT Math Answers Explained (With Steps)
chunks.text:
Representative problem: A town's population grew by 150% between 2016 and 2026, then fell by 50% the next year. What was the overall percent change from 2016?
"Grew by 150%" means 250% of the original: multiplier 250/100 = 2.5.
"Fell by 50%" means half remains: multiplier 50/100 = 0.5.
Chain: 2.5 × 0.5 = 1.25 — the town is at 125% of its 2016 population, a 25% overall increase .
Many students computed 150 − 50 = 100 and answered "a 100% increase" — the add-the-percents error in disguise. Others assumed a 50% fall must undo the growth and answered "back to the original," confusing "fell by 50%" with "fell by 150%." The rule: "increased by N%" means ×(1 + N/100); "decreased by N%" means ×(1 − N/100). Chain the multipliers and the debate ends.
# The extraneous-solution algebra trap
Another heavily debated type was the equation that punishes students who skip the final check:
Representative problem: Solve √(x + 5) = x − 1.
Square both sides: x + 5 = (x − 1)² = x² − 2x + 1.
Rearrange: 0 = x² − 3x − 4 = (x − 4)(x + 1), so x = 4 or x = −1.

chunks.title: October 2026 SAT Math Answers Explained (With Steps)
chunks.text:
Check both in the original — squaring can manufacture fake answers. For x = 4: √(9) = 3 and 4 − 1 = 3 ✓. For x = −1: √(4) = 2 but −1 − 1 = −2 ✗. Since 2 ≠ −2, x = −1 is extraneous.
Why did students split? Many stopped at "x = 4 or x = −1" and selected both — or, under time pressure, circled only −1. On the SAT, whenever you square both sides or multiply by an expression containing x, the check step is the actual question — and the test writers know tired students skip it.
# Desmos-eligible: where two graphs meet
Several debated questions were intersection problems — exactly what the on-screen Desmos calculator was made for:
Representative problem: The graphs of y = x² − 4x + 3 and y = −x + 7 intersect at two points. What is the product of the x-coordinates of the intersection points?
In Desmos, graph both equations and click each intersection: (4, 3) and (−1, 8). The product of the x-coordinates is 4 × (−1) = −4. Thirty seconds, zero algebra, no sign-error-prone factoring step.

chunks.title: October 2026 SAT Math Answers Explained (With Steps)
chunks.text:
Set the expressions equal: x² − 4x + 3 = −x + 7, so x² − 3x − 4 = 0, giving x = 4 or x = −1. Product: 4 × (−1) = −4 — matching Desmos exactly. Students who graphed first caught their own factoring mistakes before submitting: on the digital SAT the calculator is part of the intended solution path.
# How to check your SAT math work with Desmos
You do not need to master all of Desmos — a short checklist covers nearly every debated question type from October:
Graph both sides of any equation. Enter each side as a function; the intersections are your solutions. A hand-found "solution" that is not an intersection is extraneous.
Use the table for exact values instead of estimating from screen pixels.
Test each answer choice. Substitute every candidate into the original equation — e.g., evaluate √(−1 + 5) − (−1 − 1) and see which gives zero.
Watch for blank spots on the graph. Desmos will not plot the square root of a negative number or a division by zero. A gap in the graph warns that your algebraic answer may be invalid there.
Type percent chains as one multiplication: 0.75 × 0.8 × 1000 confirms the 600 before you commit to an answer.
# What to practice next

chunks.text:
The October 2026 debates point to three skills: chaining percents without adding them, checking every solution in the original equation, and verifying with Desmos. Drill them with the free tools on this site. The equation solver with steps walks through radical and quadratic equations line by line — ideal for practicing the extraneous-solution check until it becomes a reflex. The algebra calculator handles factoring, simplification, and quick numeric verification. The percentage calculator is handy for drilling chained-percent problems until the multipliers feel automatic, and the quadratic equation solver covers the factoring behind the intersection questions. Work ten chained-percent problems and ten "solve, then check" equations this week, and the next viral thread will be one you are explaining — not one you are arguing in.

By Reddit volume: the "p/1000" percent-chain question, debated by 53 students with answers splitting across 600, 550, 650, and 700. The hard part was not the arithmetic — it was seeing that each percent applies to a new base, so the percents must be chained, not added.

chunks.text:

Yes. Chaining the multipliers — (75/100) × (80/100) × 1,000 in our representative reconstruction — gives 600. The top wrong answer, 550, came from adding the percents (25% + 20% = 45%) instead of chaining them.
# Why did so many students choose 550, 650, or 700?
Each maps to a classic trap: 550 from adding chained percents instead of multiplying, 700 from the wrong base, 650 from a stale number. SAT percent questions are engineered around exactly these three slips.
